definition: Real-time data (RTD) is information that is delivered immediately after collection.
details: There is no delay in the timeliness of the information provided. Real-time data is often used for navigation or tracking. Such data is usually processed using real-time computing although it can also be stored for later or off-line data analysis. Real-time data is not the same as dynamic data. Real-time data can be dynamic (e.g. a variable indicating current location) or static (e.g. a fresh log entry indicating location at a specific time).

explainer.lead: Real-time data is information delivered immediately after collection, with no delay in its timeliness. It matters for navigation and tracking, where stale information is useless.

tiers.eli5: Like a live sports score that updates the moment something happens, not the next day's newspaper.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers stream such data through real-time computing, while also storing it for later analysis. Pitfall: confusing real-time with dynamic—real-time data can be static, like a fresh log entry recording a location at one moment.
tiers.paperLevel: Data whose delivery latency after collection is effectively zero; it may be dynamic (a variable holding current position) or static (a fixed record of a past instant). It is defined by timeliness of delivery, not by whether the value changes.

explainer.example: A delivery app shows a driver's position updating as it is collected, rather than on an hourly refresh.
